events.title: Temple of Vortumnus on the Aventine
events.summary: Marcus Fulvius Flaccus, consul 264, triumphed over Volsinii on 1 November 264 and built a temple on the Aventine to Vortumnus, the chief god of the Volsinians, whom he had 'called out' (evocatio) before the sack. A painting of Flaccus in triumphal dress decorated the temple.
events.detail: The evocatio of Vortumnus is one of the clearest Republican examples of the ritual by which a besieged city's patron god was promised a better cult at Rome. Pliny says the Romans carried off 2,000 bronze statues from Volsinii. A dedicatory base found in the area of Sant'Omobono in the Forum Boarium, inscribed with Flaccus' name and 'Volsinio capto', was probably a display of the spoils. The old city was destroyed and its people moved to a new site at Volsinii Novi (Bolsena).

events.title: Duilius relieves Segesta and storms Macella
events.summary: After Mylae, Duilius landed in Sicily, raised the Carthaginian siege of Segesta, an Elymian city which had joined Rome claiming Trojan kinship, and took Macella by storm. His inscription on the Columna Rostrata lists both successes before the naval victory.

events.title: Duilius' temple of Janus in the Forum Holitorium
events.summary: From the spoils of Mylae, Gaius Duilius built a temple of Janus near the Theatre of Marcellus in the vegetable market. Tiberius restored it in AD 17. It is usually identified with one of the three Republican temples incorporated in the church of San Nicola in Carcere.
events.debate: Assignment of the three temples under San Nicola in Carcere (Janus, Spes, Juno Sospita) is disputed.

events.title: Temple of the Tempestates vowed after a storm off Corsica
events.summary: Lucius Cornelius Scipio, consul 259, caught in a storm during his Corsican campaign, vowed a temple to the Weather Goddesses and built it near the Porta Capena. His epitaph in the Tomb of the Scipios records that he took Corsica and Aleria and 'gave a temple to the Tempestates, deservedly'.

events.title: Calatinus takes Hippana, Mytistratus, Camarina and Enna
events.summary: The consul Aulus Atilius Calatinus cleared central and southern Sicily: he stormed Hippana, took Mytistratus (which had resisted for seven months in 260) and sold its people, besieged Camarina with siege engines borrowed from Hiero and sold the inhabitants, and captured Enna by treachery.

events.title: Regulus' army and the serpent of the Bagradas
events.summary: Roman tradition held that Regulus' army, camped on the Bagradas, had to kill with siege artillery a serpent 120 feet long that was carrying off soldiers who went for water; its skin and jaws were displayed in a temple at Rome until the Numantine War.
events.debate: The story comes through Aelius Tubero via Gellius and Valerius Maximus; Polybius does not mention it. It may be a moralising tale or an elaboration of a large python seen in Africa.

events.title: Aurelius Cotta takes Thermae and Lipara
events.summary: The consul Gaius Aurelius Cotta captured Thermae Himeraeae and the Carthaginian naval base of Lipara, using ships borrowed from Hiero. When his kinsman Publius Aurelius Pecuniola let the siege works at Lipara be burned in his absence, Cotta had him flogged and reduced to the ranks.

sides.strength: consular army with borrowed Syracusan ships

battle.significance: Removed the last Carthaginian naval base north of Sicily.

events.title: Alexon the Achaean foils a mercenary plot at Lilybaeum
events.summary: Early in the siege of Lilybaeum, mercenary officers of the garrison agreed to betray the city to the Romans. Alexon, an Achaean who had already saved Agrigentum from a similar betrayal, warned the commander Himilco, who won the troops back with promises of pay before the conspirators could act.

events.title: Greek mercenaries burn the Roman siege works at Lilybaeum
events.summary: When a violent wind sprang up, some Greek mercenaries of the Lilybaeum garrison suggested a night sortie; they fired the Roman towers, rams and penthouses from upwind, and the smoke and flames blinded the defenders. Rome gave up storming the city and settled for a blockade by land, which lasted to the end of the war.

battle.significance: Turned the siege of Lilybaeum from assault to a nine-year blockade.

events.title: Hannibal the Rhodian runs the blockade of Lilybaeum
events.summary: A Carthaginian noble known as the Rhodian repeatedly sailed his fast ship through the shoals into Lilybaeum and out again by daylight, challenging the Roman fleet to catch him. The Romans eventually blocked the channel with a mole, captured a four-banker that ran aground, used it to catch the Rhodian, and later copied his ship for their final fleet.

battle.significance: Supplied the model for the quinqueremes built in 242.

events.title: Junius Pullus seizes Mount Eryx
events.summary: After losing his convoy, the consul Lucius Junius Pullus surprised the summit of Mount Eryx with its famous temple of Aphrodite and the town halfway down, establishing a post that would watch Drepana and later sandwich Hamilcar Barca's force on the mountain.

events.title: Hamilcar Barca raids Locri and Bruttium
events.summary: On taking command in 247, Hamilcar Barca opened with a seaborne raid on the coast of Italy around Locri and Bruttium before seizing Heircte near Panormus. Carthaginian raids continued to reach as far as Cumae in the following years.

events.title: Hanno the Great takes Hecatompylus (Theveste)
events.summary: While Hamilcar fought in Sicily, Carthage's African expansionists under Hanno pushed into the interior and took Hecatompylus, 'the city of a hundred gates', usually identified with Theveste. Diodorus says Hanno took 3,000 hostages and spared the city when its elders came out as suppliants.
events.debate: Identification with Theveste rests on later Greek usage; the rivalry between Hanno's African policy and the Barcid Sicilian war is a modern reconstruction from Polybius 1.67-74 and Appian.

events.title: Census of 247: 241,212 citizens
events.summary: The censors of 247 registered 241,212 citizens, against 297,797 at the lustrum of 252. The fall of over 50,000 reflects the slaughter of Ecnomus, Tunes, Drepana and especially the fleet disasters off Camarina and Palinurus, in which the rowers and marines drowned by the tens of thousands.
events.debate: Whether the census figures (adult male citizens) are complete is debated: absentees on service may have gone unregistered, which would exaggerate the drop (Brunt, Italian Manpower).

events.title: Trial of Claudia for insulting the Roman people
events.summary: Claudia, sister of Publius Claudius Pulcher (the loser of Drepana), was jostled by the crowd leaving the games and said she wished her brother were alive to lose another fleet and thin out the mob. The plebeian aediles Gaius Fundanius and Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus fined her 25,000 asses of heavy bronze.
events.detail: Gellius, citing Ateius Capito, treats the case as the first prosecution of a woman for words against the maiestas of the Roman people. It belongs to a series of aedilician prosecutions before the people which show the aediles acting as public prosecutors in the mid-Republic, and it fed the later annalistic picture of the Claudii as arrogant. The fine was paid in aes grave, a reminder that Rome's main accounting unit was still heavy cast bronze.

events.title: Lutatius Catulus seizes the harbour of Drepana
events.summary: With 200 new quinqueremes, the consul Gaius Lutatius Catulus occupied the harbour of Drepana and the anchorages near Lilybaeum in summer 242, cutting the Carthaginian garrisons and Hamilcar's army on Eryx off by sea. Wounded in the thigh while assaulting Drepana, he spent the winter training his crews.

battle.significance: Forced Carthage to send a relief fleet, leading to the Aegates.

events.title: Lutatius Catulus builds a temple of Juturna
events.summary: Gaius Lutatius Catulus, victor of the Aegates, dedicated a temple to the nymph Juturna in the Campus Martius. It is often identified with Temple A of the Largo Argentina, though some scholars prefer to give that temple to Feronia or to Lutatius Catulus' later kinsman.
events.debate: The identification of the Largo Argentina temples (A: Juturna, C: Feronia, D: Lares Permarini?) remains disputed (Coarelli vs others).

events.title: Latin colony at Spoletium
events.summary: Rome founded a Latin colony at Spoletium in Umbria, on the route that the Via Flaminia would later follow. In 217, after Trasimene, it repulsed Hannibal's assault; the Porta Fuga was later said to commemorate his flight.

events.title: Triumphs of Lutatius Catulus and Valerius Falto
events.summary: The Fasti record naval triumphs over the Carthaginians for the consul Gaius Lutatius Catulus on 4 October 241 and for the praetor Quintus Valerius Falto on 6 October. Falto had claimed the victory because the consul was lying wounded; the dispute was decided in Catulus' favour by a formal wager (sponsio) judged by Atilius Calatinus.
events.detail: Valerius Maximus gives the argument: the consul held the auspices and the summum imperium, so a victory under them was his even if he was absent from the fighting. The case is a key text for the doctrine that triumphs belonged to the holder of the auspices, and for the use of private-law sponsio procedure to settle a public quarrel. Both men triumphed anyway, an indication of how readily the Senate granted triumphs in the third century.

events.title: Hanno the Great fails to relieve Utica
events.summary: Hanno, commanding Carthage's army against the rebel mercenaries besieging Utica, routed them with his elephants and seized their camp, but then let his men disperse; the rebels rallied and retook the camp. Carthage replaced him with Hamilcar Barca.

battle.significance: Discredited Hanno and brought Hamilcar back to command.

events.title: Battle of the Bagradas
events.summary: Hamilcar Barca, with 10,000 men and 70 elephants, slipped out of the blockaded isthmus of Carthage by crossing the Bagradas mouth when wind piled sand across it, then drew the rebels under Spendius into an attack by feigning retreat, wheeled about and killed some 6,000.
events.locName: Mouth of the Bagradas near Utica

battle.significance: First major Carthaginian success of the Mercenary War.

events.title: First Latin play at the Ludi Romani
events.summary: At the Ludi Romani of 240, the year after the victory over Carthage, Livius Andronicus, a Greek from Tarentum, staged the first Latin play adapted from a Greek original. Cicero and Gellius, following Atticus and Varro, date the start of Roman literature to this production.
events.detail: Livius, said to have been brought to Rome as a captive after the fall of Tarentum (272) and freed by a Livius Salinator, also translated the Odyssey into Saturnian verse (Odusia), which remained a school text until Horace's day. Accius placed his first play much later, in 197, a dating Cicero rejected. The 240 production reflects the confidence and Hellenising mood after the First Punic War: games were extended to include drama on the Greek model, and Latin acquired a literary language through translation. Livy (7.2) adds that Livius acted in his own plays and, when his voice failed, had a boy sing the cantica while he mimed.
scholarship: Feeney, Beyond Greek: The Beginnings of Latin Literature (2016)
Goldberg, Constructing Literature in the Roman Republic (2005)
events.debate: Accius' dating to 197 and the captivity story are rejected by most scholars; Feeney stresses how unusual it was for a society to translate another's literature systematically.

events.title: Torture of Gesco and the Carthaginian prisoners
events.summary: To make reconciliation with Carthage impossible after Hamilcar's offers of clemency drew men away, Spendius, Autaritus and Mathos had Gesco and about 700 Carthaginian prisoners mutilated, their limbs broken, and thrown alive into a ditch. Polybius calls the war that followed 'truceless' (aspondos).

events.title: Rome refuses Utica and helps Carthage against the rebels
events.summary: Despite a quarrel over 500 Italian traders arrested for supplying the rebels, Rome kept faith with the treaty of 241: it returned the remaining Carthaginian prisoners of war without ransom, banned trade with the rebels while allowing it with Carthage, let Hiero supply Carthage, and refused offers of surrender from Utica and from the mercenaries in Sardinia.
events.debate: Polybius contrasts this correctness with the seizure of Sardinia a year later, which he calls contrary to all justice (3.28).

events.title: Final defeat and execution of Mathos
events.summary: Reconciled by their senate, Hamilcar and Hanno jointly brought Mathos' remaining army to a pitched battle in the east of Carthaginian Africa and destroyed it. Mathos was led through Carthage in a triumph of torture; Utica and Hippo Acra surrendered soon after, ending the war after three years and four months.

battle.significance: Ended the Mercenary War; Carthage free to turn to Spain.

events.debate: Polybius names Leptis only as a place where Mathos was earlier blockaded; the battlefield is unknown.

events.title: First Roman campaigns against the Ligurians
events.summary: From 238 consuls campaigned against the Ligurians of the northern Apennines, partly to protect Pisae and the coastal route to Spain. Publius Cornelius Lentulus Caudinus triumphed over them in 236 and Quintus Fabius Maximus, in his first consulship, in 233, vowing a temple to Honos.

events.title: Boii and Transalpine Gauls march on Ariminum
events.summary: A new generation of Boii, Polybius says, invited Gauls from beyond the Alps and advanced on Ariminum. A Roman army marched out, but the Boian rank and file, distrusting the newcomers, killed their own kings Atis and Galatus and fought the Transalpines, so the invasion collapsed without a battle with Rome.

events.title: Naevius stages his first play
events.summary: Gnaeus Naevius, a Campanian veteran of the First Punic War, produced his first drama in 235. He wrote comedies and tragedies on Greek models, invented the fabula praetexta on Roman subjects (Clastidium, on Marcellus' victory of 222), and in old age composed the Bellum Punicum, the first Latin epic on Roman history.

events.title: Wars in Sardinia and Corsica
events.summary: Rome spent five years subduing the interior of its new islands. Titus Manlius Torquatus triumphed over the Sardinians in 235 and closed the temple of Janus; Spurius Carvilius triumphed in 234; Manius Pomponius Matho in 233 hunted Sardinian fugitives in the mountains with dogs brought from Italy; Papirius Maso fought in Corsica in 231.

events.title: Census of 234: 270,713 citizens
events.summary: The census of 234 recorded 270,713 citizens, a recovery from 241,212 in 247 and 260,000 in 241 as the generation lost at sea was replaced and the new tribes Velina and Quirina were filled.

events.title: Fabius Maximus' temple of Honos
events.summary: Quintus Fabius Maximus dedicated a temple to Honos (the deified idea of military honour) outside the Porta Capena from his Ligurian spoils. Marcellus later sought to add Virtus to the same building, provoking the pontifical ruling that one cella could not serve two deities.

events.title: Spurius Carvilius Ruga and the first divorce
events.summary: Roman antiquarians dated the first divorce at Rome to around 230: Spurius Carvilius Ruga dismissed his much-loved wife because she bore him no children, after the censors had required citizens to swear that they married to beget children. The case prompted the first legal arrangements for the return of dowries (cautiones rei uxoriae).
scholarship: Watson, The Law of Persons in the Later Roman Republic (1967)
events.debate: Gellius gives the consuls of 227, Dionysius the 520th year of the city (231/0), Valerius Maximus 604 AUC. Watson and Treggiari doubt it was truly the first divorce; more likely the first without fault on the wife's part, and the origin of the actio rei uxoriae.

events.title: Earthquake at Rhodes; fall of the Colossus
events.summary: A great earthquake threw down the Colossus of Rhodes, the walls and the dockyards. Polybius lists the gifts that poured in from Hiero and Gelon of Syracuse, Ptolemy III, Antigonus Doson, Seleucus III and others, and comments that the Rhodians turned disaster into profit by their skill in appeals.
events.debate: Dated 227 or 226 (Eusebius has 228/7). The Colossus lay where it fell for nearly 900 years; Ptolemy offered to pay for re-erection but an oracle forbade it.

events.title: The quadrigatus silver and the oath-scene gold
events.summary: In the years before and during the early Second Punic War Rome struck a silver didrachm showing a Janus head and Jupiter in a four-horse chariot (the quadrigatus), with the legend ROMA, alongside rare gold staters and half-staters showing two warriors swearing an oath over a pig. The quadrigatus was steadily debased and abandoned when the denarius was introduced.
events.detail: Livy mentions argentum quadrigatum and bigatum as standard silver in the Cannae ransom negotiations. Hoard evidence shows quadrigati losing fineness from about 97% to well under 50% silver as war costs mounted, part of the monetary crisis that ended with the denarius reform of about 211. The oath-scene gold probably marks a moment of alliance (perhaps the mobilisation of 225 or Rome's Italian alliance in 216); its type was copied by the Italian rebels in 90. Crawford's Roman Republican Coinage (RRC 28-29) is the standard catalogue.
scholarship: Burnett, Coinage in the Roman World (1987)
events.debate: Start date disputed: Crawford puts the quadrigatus c. 225-212; others start it c. 235.

events.title: Battle of Sellasia
events.summary: Antigonus III Doson, leading Macedonians, Achaeans and the Hellenic Symmachy (about 28,000 foot and 1,200 horse), defeated Cleomenes III of Sparta (about 20,000) on the hills of Euas and Olympus north of Sparta. The young Philopoemen distinguished himself by charging without orders. Sparta was occupied for the first time in its history.
events.detail: Polybius, who knew veterans of the battle and had Aratus' memoirs, gives a detailed account: Cleomenes held two hills flanking the road, his brother Eucleidas on Euas and himself on Olympus. Illyrians and Achaeans attacked Euas; Cleomenes' mercenaries got behind them until Philopoemen, a young cavalryman, attacked without orders and broke the light troops; Eucleidas was then driven off his hill. Cleomenes then charged with his phalanx and was crushed by the double-depth Macedonian phalanx. He fled to Alexandria. The victory made Macedon the arbiter of Greece just as Rome first crossed the Adriatic, and set up the alliance system that Philip V would lead into the Social War of 220.

battle.significance: Restored Macedonian hegemony in the Peloponnese, which Philip V inherited.

events.title: Hannibal's first campaigns: the Olcades
events.summary: In his first season of command Hannibal attacked the Olcades in central Spain, stormed their chief town (Polybius' Althaea, Livy's Cartala) and wintered at New Carthage with his army well paid. In 220 he struck at the Vaccaei, taking Helmantica and Arbucala, and won at the Tagus on the way back.

events.title: Defeat of the satrap Molon
events.summary: Antiochus III, king since 223, marched against Molon, satrap of Media, who had defeated two royal armies and taken Seleucia on the Tigris. In the battle near Apollonia Molon's left wing defected to the king at the first contact; Molon killed himself. Antiochus then purged his minister Hermeias.

battle.significance: Secured the eastern satrapies for the young Antiochus III.

events.title: War of Rhodes and Byzantium over the Bosporus tolls
events.summary: Byzantium, paying tribute to the Gauls of Tylis, imposed a toll on ships passing the Bosporus. Rhodes, speaking for the Aegean trading cities, went to war in alliance with Prusias I of Bithynia; within a year Byzantium gave way and abolished the dues.
events.detail: Polybius' digression on the Black Sea trade (4.38-45) is the best ancient account of the grain, slaves, honey, hides and salt fish shipped through the Straits, and of the Byzantines' plight between Thracian raiders and maritime customers. The war shows Rhodes acting as a policeman of free navigation, the role it would later play against Philip V and which Rome undercut in 166.

events.title: Ludi Plebeii first attested
events.summary: The Plebeian Games, held in November and organised by the plebeian aediles, are first securely attested in the 210s; a late tradition connects them with Gaius Flaminius and his circus of 220. Livy records them being repeated (instauratio) for ritual faults in 216 and 213.
events.debate: Pseudo-Asconius dates them to the regal period or the first secession; most moderns put their institution c. 220 (Taylor, Wiseman).

events.title: Archagathus, the first Greek doctor at Rome
events.summary: According to Cassius Hemina, the Peloponnesian doctor Archagathus came to Rome in 219, was granted citizenship and a surgery bought at public expense at the Compitum Acilium. His enthusiasm for cutting and cautery soon earned him the name 'carnifex' (butcher).

events.title: Clastidium and its granary betrayed to Hannibal
events.summary: Short of supplies after the Ticinus, Hannibal obtained Clastidium, a Roman supply base south of the Po, when its commander Dasius of Brundisium handed it over for 400 gold pieces. Hannibal treated the garrison well to advertise his mildness towards Rome's allies.

events.title: Hannibal storms Victumulae
events.summary: In the winter after the Trebia, Hannibal was wounded in an attack on a Roman trading post near Placentia, then stormed Victumulae, a fortified market town that had armed the local population against him, and sacked it.
events.debate: Known only from Livy; Polybius is silent and some suspect annalistic invention.

events.title: Prodigies and expiations of winter 218/217
events.summary: After the Trebia, Livy lists a cascade of portents: a six-month-old child shouted 'Io triumphe' in the vegetable market, an ox climbed to the third storey of a house, phantom ships shone in the sky, the temple of Hope was struck by lightning. The Senate ordered a lustration of the city, a lectisternium for Juventas and a supplication at the temple of Hercules.
events.detail: Livy's prodigy lists, drawn from the annales of the pontiffs, cluster in crisis years like 218-217, 214 and 207. They show the state's apparatus for absorbing fear: the Senate received reports, referred them to the pontiffs, haruspices or the decemviri sacris faciundis, and ordered the appropriate expiation. Rawson and Rasmussen argue the lists are broadly authentic records rather than literary colour.
scholarship: Rasmussen, Public Portents in Republican Rome (2003)

events.title: Condemnation of Livius Salinator
events.summary: Marcus Livius Salinator, consul 219 and victor in the Second Illyrian War, was convicted by the people of unfair division of the booty. All the tribes except the Maecia voted against him; he withdrew to his estates for years before returning to win the Metaurus in 207 and, as censor in 204, to punish the 34 tribes.
events.debate: The year (218 or slightly later) and whether Aemilius Paullus, his colleague in 219, was also accused are uncertain.

events.title: The Spanish hostages at Saguntum
events.summary: Publius Scipio joined his brother in Spain with 20 ships and 8,000 men; the brothers crossed the Ebro and camped near Saguntum, where Hannibal had left the hostages of the Iberian peoples. A Spanish noble, Abilyx, persuaded the Carthaginian commander Bostar to release them to him, then handed them to the Scipios, who sent them home and won over many tribes.

events.title: Destruction of Centenius' cavalry near Lake Plestina
events.summary: Days after Trasimene, 4,000 cavalry sent ahead by the consul Servilius Geminus under the propraetor Gaius Centenius were intercepted by Maharbal in the Umbrian uplands; half were killed and the rest surrendered the next day.

battle.significance: Stripped the remaining consular army of its cavalry and deepened the panic after Trasimene.

events.title: Servilius Geminus' naval raid on Africa
events.summary: With 120 ships, the consul Servilius Geminus sailed round Sardinia and Corsica to Africa, extracted 10 talents from the island of Cercina, ravaged Meninx (Djerba), and lost about 1,000 men to an ambush on the African mainland before returning via Lilybaeum.

events.title: Lex Flaminia minus solvendi
events.summary: Festus records a lex Flaminia 'minus solvendi' of 217 by which debts expressed in the old heavy bronze could be settled with lighter coin, a measure tied to the reduction of the as during the war (Pliny puts the uncial as in Fabius' dictatorship of 217).
events.debate: Pliny's chronology of the as reductions is generally rejected: the sextantal as is now tied to the denarius reform of c. 211 and the uncial as to c. 141 (Crawford). Whether the lex was a debt relief law or a coinage law is debated.

events.title: Lex Minucia: the three public bankers
events.summary: Amid the post-Cannae financial crisis, the tribune Marcus Minucius carried a law creating three public bankers (triumviri mensarii), who managed state payments and loans; the board was enlarged to five in 214. Livy calls it a measure forced by 'scarcity of money'.

events.title: The Senate refuses to ransom the Cannae prisoners
events.summary: Hannibal sent ten of the 8,000 Romans captured at Cannae to Rome with Carthalo to negotiate a ransom of three minae a head (Polybius; Livy gives 300 quadrigati for a foot soldier). After a debate in which Titus Manlius Torquatus spoke against, the Senate refused; Hannibal sold most of the prisoners into slavery.
events.detail: Polybius, writing his book 6 analysis of the constitution, uses the refusal as proof of Roman resolve: the Senate deprived Hannibal of funds and taught its soldiers that they must win or die. Livy builds Torquatus' speech around the claim that the prisoners had failed to break out when others did. One of the ten tried to evade his oath to return by going back to Hannibal's camp on a pretext; the Senate sent him back in chains. Cicero turns the episode into a lesson on oaths. Many of the enslaved Romans surfaced in Greece in 194, when the Achaeans bought 1,200 of them back as a gift for Flamininus.

events.title: The legions of Cannae banished to Sicily
events.summary: The survivors of Cannae, organised into two legions, were sent to garrison Sicily and forbidden to return to Italy or be discharged until the war was over. Twice denied pardon by the Senate, they fought under Marcellus at Syracuse and finally redeemed themselves with Scipio in Africa.
events.detail: Livy gives their petition of 212 to Marcellus, recalling that the consul Varro, who fled, was thanked by the Senate while they were punished. In 209 the survivors of the two disastrous battles of Herdonia joined them under the same conditions. Scipio picked the best of them in 205 for his African expedition; at Zama they formed part of his veteran core. Their decade-long humiliation is often cited as an extreme example of Roman military discipline and of the Senate's use of shame.

events.title: Siege of Petelia
events.summary: The small Bruttian town of Petelia refused to join Hannibal after Cannae and held out for eleven months against Himilco and the Bruttians, eating leather, bark and grass, after Rome told its envoys it could not help. It finally surrendered in 215; Rome later rewarded the survivors.

battle.significance: A celebrated example of loyalty among Rome's allies.

events.title: Temple of Concordia on the Arx
events.summary: The praetor Lucius Manlius had vowed a temple to Concord during a mutiny of his troops in Gaul in 218; it was dedicated on the Arx on 5 February 216 by duumviri appointed for the purpose.

events.title: Temples of Mens and Venus Erycina on the Capitol
events.summary: Vowed after Trasimene on the advice of the Sibylline Books, temples to Mens (Right Thinking) and to Venus of Eryx were dedicated on the Capitol in 215, Mens by Titus Otacilius Crassus and Venus Erycina by Quintus Fabius Maximus. The Sicilian goddess of the mountain held by Rome in the First Punic War became a Roman state cult.

events.title: Massacre at Hamae and the defence of Cumae
events.summary: The Campanians planned to seize Cumae during a joint nocturnal festival at Hamae. Warned, the consul Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus fell on their camp at midnight and killed some 2,000, including their commander Marius Alfius. Hannibal then besieged Gracchus in Cumae but was beaten off.

battle.significance: Kept Cumae and its harbour for Rome.

events.title: Second battle of Nola
events.summary: Marcellus again repulsed Hannibal outside Nola. Livy reports 5,000 Carthaginians killed against fewer than 1,000 Romans, figures most scholars doubt; the substance is that Hannibal failed to win Nola, which remained a Roman base for the rest of the war.

battle.significance: Kept Nola Roman.

events.title: Bruttians take Croton; Locri defects
events.summary: The Bruttians, now Hannibal's allies, besieged Croton, a shadow of its old size with fewer than 20,000 citizens; Hanno negotiated its surrender and the Greek citizens moved to Locri, which had itself gone over to Carthage. Rhegium alone of the Greek cities of the toe stayed Roman.

events.title: Relief of Iliturgi and Intibili
events.summary: After Ibera, Livy says the Scipios relieved Iliturgi, besieged by three Carthaginian armies, killing 16,000, and then won again at Intibili. The figures and perhaps the battles derive from the inflated annalist Valerius Antias.
events.debate: Iliturgi and Intibili are far apart and the inland campaign implied is hard to fit before 212; many treat these victories as doublets or exaggerations.

events.title: Third battle of Nola
events.summary: For the third time Hannibal tried to take Nola and was checked by Marcellus in an indecisive engagement; Claudius Nero's cavalry, sent round to take Hannibal in the rear, failed to arrive in time.

battle.significance: Third failure before Nola.

events.title: Fabius and Marcellus recapture Casilinum
events.summary: Casilinum, which Hannibal had taken in 215 after a heroic defence, was retaken by Fabius Maximus and Marcellus; the 2,000 Campanian and 700 Carthaginian defenders were allowed to leave under truce, but Marcellus' troops cut down many as they came out.

events.title: Assassination of Hieronymus and the Syracusan revolution
events.summary: Hieronymus, king of Syracuse at fifteen, was murdered at Leontini by conspirators. In Syracuse the people restored a republic, then massacred the royal family, including Hiero's daughters Damarata and Heraclia and Heraclia's young daughters. Hippocrates and Epicydes won the generalship and broke with Rome.
events.detail: Livy's account of the Syracusan revolution of 214 is one of the fullest narratives of Hellenistic civic stasis in Latin. Andranodorus, Hiero's son-in-law, tried to seize power and was killed in the senate house; the assembly then ordered the deaths of the royal women. Polybius criticises historians who wrote melodrama about Hieronymus' cruelty. The upshot was Syracuse's alignment with Carthage, which brought on Marcellus' siege.

events.title: Marcellus storms Leontini
events.summary: Marcellus took Leontini, held by Hippocrates, at the first assault and beheaded some 2,000 Roman deserters found there. Hippocrates and Epicydes spread the story at Syracuse that the Romans had massacred the townspeople, which swung Syracuse decisively against Rome.

events.title: Massacre at Henna
events.summary: Fearing that the people of Henna would betray the town to Carthage, the Roman commander Lucius Pinarius summoned an assembly in the theatre and had his soldiers kill the unarmed citizens. Marcellus condoned the act, and the sacrilege at the sanctuary town of Ceres turned more Sicilians against Rome.

events.title: Censors punish the defeatists of Cannae
events.summary: The censors Marcus Atilius Regulus and Publius Furius Philus degraded Lucius Caecilius Metellus, who after Cannae had talked of abandoning Italy, together with prisoners who had broken their oath to return, and about 2,000 young men who had dodged service, sending the latter to Sicily to serve with the Cannae legions.

events.title: Siege of Sardis and the death of Achaeus
events.summary: Antiochus III besieged his rebel cousin Achaeus in Sardis; the lower city fell in 215/4 when a Cretan, Lagoras, saw vultures perched on an unguarded cliff and led an escalade there. Achaeus held the citadel until the Cretan Bolis, pretending to rescue him for Sosibius, betrayed him in 213. He was mutilated and crucified.

battle.significance: Restored Seleucid control of Asia Minor, freeing Antiochus for his eastern anabasis.

events.title: Battles of Munda and Auringis
events.summary: Livy records victories of the Scipios over Hasdrubal Barca and Mago near Munda and Auringis in southern Spain, with Gnaeus Scipio wounded in the thigh. The scale and even the location of these battles are suspect, but the Scipios were active in the south by this date.

events.title: Recapture of Arpi
events.summary: The consul Quintus Fabius Maximus, son of the Cunctator, entered Arpi at night in a rainstorm that drowned the noise of his men scaling the walls. The townsmen, after negotiating, turned on the 5,000-strong Carthaginian garrison; the Spaniards among it changed sides, and the rest were allowed to go to Hannibal.

battle.significance: First major Roman recovery of a defected Apulian city.

events.title: The Scipios ally with Syphax
events.summary: The Scipio brothers sent three centurions to Syphax, king of the Masaesylii, who was at war with Carthage; one, Quintus Statorius, stayed to train Syphax's footsoldiers in Roman fashion. Carthage replied by allying with Gala of the Massylii, whose son Masinissa defeated Syphax.

events.title: Himilco lands in Sicily and takes Agrigentum
events.summary: Carthage sent Himilco with 25,000 foot, 3,000 horse and 12 elephants, who landed at Heraclea Minoa and recaptured Agrigentum. Many Sicilian towns, including Murgantia with its Roman grain store, went over to Carthage, and Rome's grip on the island briefly depended on the siege lines at Syracuse.

events.title: Battle of Acrillae
events.summary: Marching back to Syracuse after failing to save Agrigentum, Marcellus surprised Hippocrates' 10,000 foot and 500 horse building a camp near Acrillae and routed them, killing or capturing about 8,000.

battle.significance: Prevented a junction of the Syracusan field army with Himilco.

events.title: Philip V captures Lissus
events.summary: Having burned his fleet at the mouth of the Aous after Laevinus' night attack in 214, Philip V marched overland and in a skilful operation took the citadel of Acrolissus and then Lissus, giving Macedon an outlet on the Adriatic north of the Roman protectorate.

battle.significance: Gave Philip a base on the Adriatic and alarmed Rome.

events.title: Death of Aratus of Sicyon
events.summary: Aratus, seventeen times general of the Achaean League, died in 213, believing himself poisoned by Philip V, whom he had criticised over the outrage at Messene and the seduction of his daughter-in-law. Sicyon buried him as a hero inside the city.

events.title: Plague destroys the Carthaginian army at Syracuse
events.summary: In late summer and autumn 212 an epidemic, favoured by the marshes around the Anapus, struck both armies outside Syracuse. The Romans, quartered in the city and on higher ground, suffered less; the Carthaginian and Sicilian forces of Himilco and Hippocrates were destroyed and both commanders died.

events.title: Death of Archimedes
events.summary: When Achradina fell in 212, Archimedes, aged about 75, was killed by a Roman soldier despite Marcellus' order to spare him. Plutarch gives three versions: he was absorbed in a geometrical diagram and refused to come; he asked for time to finish a proof; he was carrying instruments a soldier took for gold. Marcellus honoured his relatives.
events.detail: Cicero, quaestor in Sicily in 75, found Archimedes' neglected tomb near the Agrigentine gate, overgrown with brambles and marked by a sphere inscribed in a cylinder, the figure Archimedes had asked for to commemorate his proof of their volume ratio. Marcellus took two of Archimedes' planetaria to Rome, one placed in the temple of Virtus. The death became a symbol of the meeting between Roman force and Greek science; the famous last words 'do not disturb my circles' are a later formulation.

events.title: Fulvius Flaccus storms Hanno's camp near Beneventum
events.summary: Hanno had gathered grain near Beneventum to revictual Capua, but the Campanians came to collect it with too few wagons. The consul Quintus Fulvius Flaccus stormed the camp; Livy claims 6,000 killed and 7,000 captured with all the grain.

battle.significance: Doomed Capua to starvation before the siege began.

events.title: Death of Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus in Lucania
events.summary: The proconsul Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, victor of Beneventum, was lured into an ambush by Flavus, a Lucanian leader who had turned to Hannibal, and killed fighting. Hannibal gave his body an honourable funeral; his slave-volunteer legions dispersed.
events.debate: Livy gives three versions of the place and circumstances.

events.title: Metapontum, Thurii and Heraclea join Hannibal
events.summary: After the fall of Tarentum, Metapontum, whose garrison had been withdrawn to the Tarentine citadel, joined Hannibal, followed by Thurii (angry at Rome's execution of its hostages) and Heraclea. Hannibal now held almost the whole Greek coast of the Gulf of Tarentum.

events.title: Scipios recapture Saguntum
events.summary: The Scipio brothers retook Saguntum, eight years after Hannibal's sack, expelled the Carthaginian garrison, restored surviving Saguntines and punished the Turdetani who had provoked the original war. Livy places it in 214, but most historians date it to 212.
events.debate: Livy's 214 conflicts with his own statement that Saguntum had been in Carthaginian hands for eight years.

events.title: Trial and exile of Gnaeus Fulvius Flaccus
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Sempronius Blaesus prosecuted the praetor of 212 for losing his army at Herdonia through negligence and running away. When the charge was turned into a capital one before the comitia centuriata, Fulvius went into exile at Tarquinii, which the people confirmed.
events.detail: Livy's account is one of the best illustrations of tribunician prosecution procedure: a series of anquisitiones before the people, a switch from a fine to a capital charge, the need for the urban praetor to fix a date for the comitia centuriata, and the defendant's right to anticipate condemnation by voluntary exile, after which a plebiscite confirmed the exile (iustum exsilium). Gnaeus' brother Quintus, then besieging Capua, tried and failed to save him.

events.title: Hasdrubal escapes at the Black Stones
events.summary: Gaius Claudius Nero, sent to Spain with 12,000 men after the deaths of the Scipios, trapped Hasdrubal Barca in a pass at the Black Stones. Hasdrubal opened negotiations to evacuate Spain, spun them out over several days and slipped his army away under cover of mist.
events.locName: Lapides Atri, between Iliturgi and Mentissa
events.debate: Many historians regard the episode as an invention to explain away Nero's failure in Spain.

events.title: Lucius Marcius rallies the remnants in Spain
events.summary: After the deaths of the Scipios, the Roman survivors north of the Ebro elected a young equestrian officer, Lucius Marcius Septimus, as their commander. He beat off Hasdrubal son of Gisco and, Livy says, stormed two Carthaginian camps. His self-styled title 'propraetor' in a dispatch to the Senate offended the fathers.
events.debate: Livy cites wildly varying casualty figures (from Claudius Quadrigarius, Valerius Antias and Piso), and the double camp victory is probably exaggerated.

events.title: Laevinus and the Aetolians take Anticyra
events.summary: Under the Roman-Aetolian treaty, Marcus Valerius Laevinus took Anticyra in Phocis and handed the town to the Aetolians while the Romans kept the movable property and the people, the first application of the treaty's grim division of spoils.

events.title: Battle of Numistro
events.summary: Marcellus, consul for the fourth time, followed Hannibal into Lucania after the second Herdonia and fought him near Numistro from the third hour until nightfall without result. Hannibal withdrew towards Apulia at night and Marcellus followed.

battle.significance: Showed Rome could again face Hannibal in the open after the Herdonia disasters.

events.title: Naval battle of Sapriportis
events.summary: A Roman squadron of 20 ships under Decimus Quinctius, bringing supplies to the besieged citadel of Tarentum, was met 15 miles from the city by an equal Tarentine fleet under Democrates. Quinctius was killed when his flagship was boarded and the Romans lost most of their ships.

battle.significance: Tightened the blockade of the Roman garrison in the citadel of Tarentum.

events.title: Salapia betrayed to Marcellus
events.summary: Blattius, a leading man of Salapia, negotiated with Marcellus to hand over the town despite his rival Dasius, the leader of the Carthaginian party. The 500 Numidian cavalry of the garrison, Hannibal's best, died fighting almost to a man, a loss Livy calls greater than the town.

events.title: Fall of Agrigentum and the end of the war in Sicily
events.summary: The consul Marcus Valerius Laevinus secured Agrigentum when Muttines, the Libyphoenician cavalry commander slighted by the Carthaginian general Hanno, opened a gate to the Romans. The leading citizens were beheaded and the rest sold. Some forty towns then surrendered, twenty were betrayed and six stormed, and Laevinus set Sicily to growing grain for Rome.

sides.losses: city taken; leaders escaped by sea

battle.significance: Ended Carthaginian resistance in Sicily; the island became Rome's granary for the rest of the war.
